resources.string: Family Radio Service: the 22 channels of bubble-pack walkie-talkies. Narrow band, low power.

General Mobile Radio Service: the same 22 channels as FRS (they talk to FRS radios) plus the 8 repeater channels 15R to 22R, which listen on 462 MHz and transmit 5 MHz higher. Channels 8 to 14 are narrow band at low power.
FCC GMRS licence needed (no exam; it covers your family)
The seven NOAA Weather Radio (and Environment Canada) broadcast channels. Receive-only; the strongest one is your local station. With SAME alerts on (PKT) the radio decodes the warnings.
Multi-Use Radio Service: five licence-free VHF channels, less crowded than FRS and reaching further outdoors. Low power (the limit is 2 W).

Marine VHF channels to listen to boats, harbours and the Coast Guard: 16 is distress and calling, 9 boater calling, 13 bridge to bridge, 22A the US Coast Guard. Receive-only: this radio is not a marine radio.
Amateur DMR simplex: the channels most DMR radios carry, all colour code 1, time slot 1, talkgroup 99.

Business itinerant channels: the \"dot\" and \"star\" frequencies that rental and store business radios come set to, used at events, shops, farms and job sites. Listening is free. On VHF this radio only works wide band, which these channels no longer allow for transmitting: talk on the UHF ones.

The 96 AAR railroad channels (02 to 97, 159.810 to 161.565 MHz; 02 to 04 are used in Canada): dispatchers, trains, yards and the trackside defect detectors that read out axle counts. Receive-only. Scan the zone to find your local railroad\'s channels, then star them.

The International Space Station and the SO-50 FM satellite, each heard for about ten minutes per pass (an app such as Heavens-Above gives the times). ISS Voice: crew contacts on 145.800 (the crew listens on 144.490 in the Americas). ISS APRS: the station\'s packet digipeater, on 437.825 since 2026 (it has used 145.825 before). ISS SSTV: picture events on 437.550 (receive only). On 70 cm the signal shifts up to 10 kHz with Doppler, so the APRS and SSTV channels come as + (rising), plain (overhead) and - (setting); PKT → ISS APRS and ISS SSTV follow the shift automatically and are the better way. ISS Rptr and SO-50 listen on 2 m and send on 70 cm, opened with a 67 Hz tone; use the + channel as the pass begins, the plain one overhead and the - one as it ends. ARISS changes the station\'s modes often: check ariss.org. Talking through a satellite with a handheld is hard: listen first. Cross-band (2 m transmit, 70 cm receive) is untested on this radio.

The 80-channel UHF CB band (476.425 to 477.4125 MHz, narrow band, 5 W). The R channels use the repeaters: they listen on 1 to 8 and 41 to 48 and transmit 750 kHz higher (on 31 to 38 and 71 to 78, which are left out as simplex channels). Channel 5 is the emergency channel (not in New Zealand), 40 the highway channel, 18 caravans and convoys, 10 four-wheel-drive clubs, 11 calling. 22 and 23 (data only) and 61 to 63 (reserved) are left out.
No licence needed in Australia and NZ; not for use in the US
PMR446, the licence-free walkie-talkie channels of Europe and the UK: 16 narrow-band channels. Low power (the limit is 0.5 W).
No licence needed in Europe; not for use in the US
Amateur FM simplex: the 2 m and 70 cm calling channels and APRS (%1$s, your region\'s APRS frequency, where the radio decodes position reports). Device → Region sets them.
Amateur FM simplex: the 2 m and 70 cm calling channels and APRS (%1$s, your region\'s APRS frequency, where the radio decodes position reports), and FM SSTV. Device → Region sets them.
Amateur FM simplex: the 2 m and 70 cm calling channels, common simplex channels and APRS (%1$s, your region\'s APRS frequency, where the radio decodes position reports). Device → Region sets them.
